items.title: Accenture Contractor Allegedly Gave Claude AI Agent Access to Secure Pentagon Network
items.summary: An Accenture employee allegedly gave a personal Claude Code AI agent administrative access to a secure U.S. Department of Defense environment, allowing it to write and deploy code. The agent reportedly operated for about two months and appears to have sent credentials and network details to an outside website. Accenture disputes the allegations, saying an independent investigation found them without merit. According to WIRED’s investigation , published October 29, the system serves multiple intelligence agencies and holds Controlled Unclassified Information, or CUI. This information is not classified, but still requires protection against unauthorized release. Claude AI Agent Allegedly Gained Access The employee reportedly connected a personal account for Anthropic’s Claude Code to a production environment on the nonclassified Internet Protocol Router Network, known as NIPRNet. Unlike classified military networks, NIPRNet connects to the internet while supporting protected government work. WIRED’s sources said the contractor shared login credentials so the agent could automate coding and cloud server setup. That reportedly gave it administrator rights and allowed it to bypass controls applied during normal login. Its work included writing code and committing changes under the employee’s identity. During those tasks, the agent appears to have transmitted passwords, login details, and a map of NIPRNet to a third-party website. WIRED withheld the site’s name and reported that NIST had identified a high-risk weakness that could let attackers inject instructions into an AI coding agent to steal credentials. The report does not establish that attackers exploited that weakness here. The concern overlaps with indirect prompt injection attacks , where hidden commands in outside content trick an agent into taking unauthorized actions. However, the exact cause of the alleged data transfer remains unclear. Security experts told WIRED that combining separate pieces of unclassified information can reveal details sensitive enough to warrant classification. A network map could also help an intruder locate valuable systems and understand how they connect. There is no indication that attackers accessed classified or top-secret networks. Former NSA hacker Jake Williams described another possible risk: stolen credentials could let attackers alter software developed on NIPRNet before it moves into more sensitive environments. A hidden backdoor could then travel with approved code. This was a potential attack path described by experts, not a confirmed outcome. Related reporting on AI agents exposing credentials highlights how routine tool use can reveal secrets without malware. Narrow permissions, short-lived credentials, and restricted network access can reduce that exposure. Accenture Rejects the Claims Accenture told WIRED that the allegations were “thoroughly and independently investigated and found to be without merit.” It said it met its legal and contractual duties but did not identify the investigator. The Pentagon declined to discuss its network status. WIRED also reported claims that Accenture did not initially notify the government. Those claims remain disputed. The publication placed Accenture’s federal contracts above $3.5 billion, including nearly $605 million with the Defense Department, underscoring the stakes of oversight across its government work. AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

items.title: CISA Warns of Linux Kernel Missing Initialization Vulnerability Exploited in Attacks
items.summary: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has warned that attackers are exploiting a Linux kernel vulnerability (CVE-2026-46300) that can help them gain control of affected systems. The flaw was added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 28, 2026, placing it among security issues with confirmed exploitation. CISA’s catalog entry sets an October 31 remediation deadline and requires forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04. The agency says attackers can chain the kernel flaw with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to implant PHP webshells and run commands as root. It remains unknown whether the vulnerability has been used in ransomware campaigns. The flaw affects how the Linux kernel combines network data held in socket buffers. According to the official CVE record, the skb_try_coalesce() function can transfer fragments backed by shared memory or the page cache without preserving the SKBFL_SHARED_FRAG marker. This marker tells later code that the data needs special handling before modification. When that marker disappears, the kernel can incorrectly treat shared fragments as safe to change directly. During Encapsulating Security Payload, or ESP, input processing, the kernel may skip a protective copying step and decrypt data in place. This can modify page-cache-backed data that should not have been changed through that path. The published CVSS score is 7.8, rated high severity. Its assessment describes a local attack requiring low privileges and no user interaction. Linux Kernel Missing Initialization Vulnerability Exploited That is important because the kernel flaw alone should not be described as an unauthenticated remote takeover. CISA’s warning instead highlights its use alongside other vulnerabilities in a broader attack chain. The upstream fix preserves the shared-fragment marker when paged fragments move between socket buffers. The CVE record identifies fixed releases across several maintained branches, including Linux 5.10.257, 5.15.208, 6.1.174, 6.6.141, 6.12.91, 6.18.33, and 7.0.10. Linux 7.1 is also listed as unaffected. Administrators should follow their Linux distribution or product vendor’s guidance when selecting updates. CISA’s entry calls for vendor-approved mitigations, checks of internet exposure, and compliance with applicable patching and forensic requirements. When mitigations aren’t available, it instructs organizations to stop using the affected product. The warning follows earlier reports of Linux kernel vulnerabilities actively exploited and a separate Linux kernel privilege escalation vulnerability exploited in attacks . Those cases also involved short remediation deadlines and forensic review, showing why patching and checking for compromise must remain separate tasks. For affected organizations, the immediate concern is the combination of confirmed exploitation, possible root access, and a tight deadline. The CISA alert makes this an urgent security response, not a routine update. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Polymarket Hacked – Users Reported Funds Stolen From Their Wallets
items.summary: Polymarket suffered a security incident on October 29, 2026, after a compromised third-party provider exposed users of its international platform to wallet theft. Traders reported missing funds, unexpected withdrawals, and positions being closed without permission. The company temporarily stopped trading, said it had fixed the issue, and promised to reimburse affected users. Trading later resumed. In its public statement , Polymarket said an outside provider had been compromised and that the matter had been referred to law enforcement. Although early descriptions pointed to an authentication provider, current reporting connects this incident to DebugBear, a website performance monitoring service. Polymarket’s own statement did not name the vendor. Malicious Script Targeted Active Trading Sessions Hudson Rock’s technical investigation found malicious JavaScript served through a DebugBear address associated with Polymarket. Instead of simply measuring page performance, the code searched for an active trading session, checked account information, and attempted to use the platform’s existing trading tools to move assets. Researchers downloaded the file twice and received identical copies. The script read browser storage containing account details, a wallet address, and trading API credentials. It then searched the application’s React components for a live trading client and its signer, the tool used to authorize wallet actions. This approach attempted to reuse access already available inside a logged-in session rather than relying on a stolen password alone. Its behavior varied by account type. One route attempted to transfer position tokens directly, while another tried to sell positions before moving available funds. Researchers also found code requesting signatures and submitting transactions through Polymarket’s relayer. However, they did not execute the sample, so the findings show intended behavior rather than proof that every attempted transfer succeeded. According to CNBC’s reporting , analysis from Betting Intelligence and Polysights linked at least $2.7 million in withdrawals to 710 wallets. These figures remain outside estimates, not an officially confirmed loss total. CNBC also reported that Polymarket’s separate United States platform was not compromised. Polymarket said affected traders would be made whole. CNBC reported that users with less than $10,000 stolen were told their funds would be restored by October 30, while larger claims would require a release form. The reimbursement pledge addresses financial losses, but the exact exposure window and initial method used to compromise the provider remain unresolved. The incident highlights risks from outside scripts running on sensitive pages. Cybersecurity News previously covered an Adform compromise that distributed crypto-stealing code , showing how trusted infrastructure can become a delivery route. Its coverage of the compromised XRPL JavaScript package describes a separate supply-chain attack aimed at wallet keys. These cases involve different theft methods, but share dependence on outside code. Users should close potentially exposed tabs, review recent orders and wallet transactions through trusted channels, and save transaction hashes for support claims. Unexpected signing requests should be rejected. Hudson Rock also recommends reviewing sessions and permissions with official support, avoiding unsolicited recovery links, and never sharing a seed phrase. Disconnecting a wallet alone does not reverse completed transfers or remove existing blockchain approvals. Users should verify compensation instructions through official channels rather than messages from unfamiliar accounts. AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

items.title: World’s Largest Crypto Exchange Binance Hacked, Over $5.7 Billion Reportedly Stolen
items.summary: Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, has suspended deposits and withdrawals while investigating a suspected security breach involving billions of dollars in digital assets. Reports suggest that around $5.7 billion may have left wallets linked to the exchange, although Binance has not confirmed the total stolen or established that every flagged transfer belongs to the attack. If verified, the incident could become the largest cryptocurrency theft on record. Update1: Binance Estimates $6.3 Billion Impact With Suspects DevOps Laptop Compromise In an official statement on X, Binance promised to cover all losses and said its teams were conducting security checks, freezing funds, and working with law enforcement. “User funds are safe,” the exchange said, adding that it would publish a full post-mortem once the investigation ends. The statement did not identify the entry point, name an attacker, or provide a reopening date. We are working non-stop to resolve this issue. Binance will cover all losses. As a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our team conducts security checks, freezes funds, and works with law enforcement. We are working around the clock and will… pic.twitter.com/zufWJ6V05D — Binance (@binance) October 30, 2026 Suspicious Transfers Span Multiple Blockchains Early reports linked the suspected Binance hack to large transfers across Ethereum, Bitcoin, and TRON. Reported outflows included approximately $1.45 billion in Bitcoin and $875 million in Ether, alongside stablecoins and other tokens. However, estimates changed as investigators examined additional wallets. Axios reported that analysts and traders placed the suspected theft between $1.7 billion and $5.7 billion, showing how uncertain the initial figures remain. That distinction matters because a wallet transfer does not, by itself, prove theft. Investigators still need to separate attacker-controlled movements from exchange activity and establish which receiving addresses belong to the same operation. Some wider estimates include Bitcoin and TRON outflows that had not yet been tied to the attacker. Treating the full reported outflow as a confirmed loss would therefore overstate the available evidence. Stablecoin issuers moved quickly to restrict funds connected to the suspected incident. According to Reuters , Tether froze nearly $1.57 billion, while Circle froze more than $800 million. Together, those actions blocked approximately $2.38 billion in stablecoins. Binance co-founder Yi He also said Ripple had frozen roughly $200 million. These figures describe frozen assets, not the total amount stolen or money already returned. Binance separately reported verified frozen assets of $2.54 billion, with tracing still underway. Freezing limits further movement, but it does not automatically restore funds to the exchange. Recovery remains a separate process. The response highlights why rapid communication between exchanges, token issuers, and investigators can reduce the damage after suspicious transfers are detected. Binance has not disclosed whether the suspected breach involved stolen signing keys, a compromised employee account, malicious software, or a weakness in its wallet systems. No public technical findings currently establish an attack path or identify a threat actor. Assigning blame before that evidence emerges would be premature. Previous exchange breaches show why the missing technical details matter. Cybersecurity News’ analysis of the Bybit attack described how attackers compromised a wallet provider’s environment and changed transaction data during a legitimate transfer. That case provides context, but it does not establish a connection to Binance or prove that the same method was used here. Binance’s promise to cover all losses is significant, but its final cost remains unknown. Reporting places its Secure Asset Fund for Users, known as SAFU, at roughly $1 billion in Bitcoin. A substantially larger confirmed shortfall could require resources beyond that emergency reserve. No detailed compensation plan has been published. The investigation also faces a familiar recovery challenge. Cybersecurity News’ report on tracing stolen Bybit funds explains how investigators combined private communications with blockchain records to identify laundering activity. For Binance, the next essential disclosures are a verified loss figure, affected wallet details, the root cause, and a safe reopening timeline. Until then, users should follow the exchange’s official updates rather than treat circulating estimates as settled facts. Update: Binance Estimates $6.3 Billion Impact, Suspects DevOps Laptop Compromise Binance has raised the estimated impact of its security incident to $6.3 billion, with around $3 billion in affected assets frozen on-chain through blockchain partners. In its latest official statement , the exchange said its initial investigation suggests a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop may have allowed an attacker to access a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance said it has found no evidence of a wallet private key leak, but stressed that the investigation remains ongoing. This is a developing story; we will keep on posted on we have updates.

items.title: KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA 2026: End User TAB recommendations and tips
items.summary: KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA 2026 in Salt Lake City will bring the cloud native community together with projects, vendors and end users in what is one of the largest open source events. In this post, we highlight content specifically targeted at end users and session recommendations from members of the CNCF End User Technical Advisory Board (TAB) , along with practical tips for making the most of the event. Birds of Feather (BoF) Newly introduced at Kubecon EU in Amsterdam back in March, we will again have a series of BoF sessions in Salt Lake City. Last time we had packed rooms discussing and brainstorming around AI infrastructure and platforms, AI observability and optimized infrastructure for training, inference and GPU efficiency. This time around we’ll open the floor to our newly formed end user groups , the TAB recently approved end user groups covering Platform Engineering, Public Sector, Telecom and Research. And in another session we will give ourselves a challenge: get end users in one room and try to build live a reference architecture for Agentic AI deployments. It’s not clear how far we will get given how fast things are moving and how different use cases can be… but it should be a good learning session and it will definitely be fun! Town Hall In Amsterdam we chose to move the End User TAB Town Hall to the project pavilion and that was well received. So we’re keeping it this way and you can come and ask us questions right next to where the projects are located. Poster sessions Did you know Kubecon has a poster session ? It’s an ideal setting to have more in-depth discussions with the authors and there are several end user focused presentations this time around. And as always, see below for recommendations on interesting content for end users from the members of the TAB. Joseph Sandoval Surviving the Churn: Read Replicas and Controllers for Busy Kubernetes Clusters (Nov 10, 12:20 PM, Salt Palace, Grand Ballroom ACE). Your apiserver is one ordered log with everyone yelling at it, and when watchers fall behind, they get 410 Gone and relist, which makes it worse. Anthropic’s war story: one innocent LIST sent a cluster of tens of thousands of nodes into a doom spiral, twice in two weeks. Some of us have the scars. N Clusters, One kubectl: Multi-Cluster That Just Works (Nov 10, 3:40 PM, Hyatt Regency, Salt Lake Ballroom C). OCM-style multi-cluster fixes the fleet problem and creates a developer problem: the hub template is the source of truth, so the kubectl scale you just ran quietly gets reverted. Salesforce and NVIDIA built a proxy that makes the fleet feel like one cluster again, kubectl edit included. Every platform fix sends a bill to somebody else, and this talk shows what it took to pay that one down. Anatomy of an Outage: When Bursty ML Workloads Break the Kubernetes Scheduler (Nov 11, 11:00 AM, Salt Palace, Grand Ballroom H). Pending workloads timed out webhooks and took down a control plane, which probably looked fine in the design review. Isomorphic Labs and Google walk through how they stabilized it with decoupled queues and Kueue tuning. I’m looking forward to reviewing the receipts. Hardening Kubernetes for GovCloud: A 3-Year Journey to FedRAMP Moderate Authorization (Nov 11, 11:50 AM, Salt Palace, Grand Ballroom ACE). Three years to an ATO sounds about right to anyone who has argued with an auditor over a deploy pipeline. Kudos to the Verkada team for building their own deployment system to meet the isolation rules, then taking on FedRAMP’s patching mandates. If you work in a regulated environment or are working on it, be front and center for the lessons learned. Juliano Martinez Zero Downtime CNI Migration at Scale: Canal to Cilium Across Hundreds of Production Clusters (Nov 10, 4:40 PM, Salt Palace, Level 1, 151). Migrating a CNI plugin in production is one of the most high-risk operations in Kubernetes infra. At Walmart running hundreds of clusters across cloud and on-premises environments, the team faced route-drop failures in Flannel beyond 300 nodes, iptables rule explosion as services grew and etcd v2 incompatibility blocking upgrades. No published playbook existed for zero-downtime CNI replacement at that scale. Saturated by Design – Maximizing Cluster Allocation in On-Premises Kubernetes (Nov 10, 11:30 AM). On-premises compute is inelastic, and the costs are mostly up-front. Yet workload demands and hardware health can change at any time. How do you make the most of your on-premises investments without risking capacity overruns and potential outages? Running Secure Agents at Scale (Nov 11, 5:00 PM, Salt Palace, Level 1, Grand Ballroom GI). Building secure and scalable agents at scale is hard. From multi-tenancy and noisy-neighbor risk to tool access and data boundaries, teams need more than a prompt and a container image; they need a deliberate execution model. From Packets to Paychecks: eBPF-Based Network Cost Attribution at Scale (Nov 12, 11:50 AM, Salt Palace, Level 1, Grand Ballroom BDF). Cloud provider bills show egress costs as a single line item-they don’t say which tenant caused them. At Adobe, we answer that across 400K pods in 31K namespaces spanning 85+ multi-tenant Kubernetes clusters using Retina eBPF agents to capture pod-level flows at the kernel. Prometheus enriches them with node topology, and a CIDR-based classifier maps each destination IP to a cost category (Local, Internet, Peering, Transit Gateway, VPC Endpoint) with cross-AZ and cross-region modifiers that align to cloud provider billing. Kenta Tada Lessons Learned Sandboxing Agents with kagent AI agents may look like ordinary Kubernetes workloads, but their long-lived, stateful, and highly privileged behavior makes sandboxing a fundamentally different challenge. This session shares lessons from building agent sandboxing with kagent, covering filesystem and tool access, credentials, networking, identity, and cleanup, along with how NVIDIA’s OpenShell, Kubernetes’ agent-sandbox, and Google’s substrate support shape the design. GPU Observability with eBPF: From Kernel Hooks to Kubernetes Metrics GPUs are becoming a critical resource in Kubernetes, yet understanding what is happening on them remains a black box. This session shows how to build production-grade GPU observability with eBPF, from hooking into GPU interfaces and enriching telemetry with Kubernetes context to packaging programs as OCI images and integrating metrics with Prometheus and OpenTelemetry. items.summary_html:
KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA 2026 in Salt Lake City will bring the cloud native community together with projects, vendors and end users in what is one of the largest open source events.

In this post, we highlight content specifically targeted at end users and session recommendations from members of the CNCF End User Technical Advisory Board (TAB), along with practical tips for making the most of the event.

Birds of Feather (BoF)

Newly introduced at Kubecon EU in Amsterdam back in March, we will again have a series of BoF sessions in Salt Lake City. Last time we had packed rooms discussing and brainstorming around AI infrastructure and platforms, AI observability and optimized infrastructure for training, inference and GPU efficiency.

This time around we’ll open the floor to our newly formed end user groups, the TAB recently approved end user groups covering Platform Engineering, Public Sector, Telecom and Research.

And in another session we will give ourselves a challenge: get end users in one room and try to build live a reference architecture for Agentic AI deployments. It’s not clear how far we will get given how fast things are moving and how different use cases can be… but it should be a good learning session and it will definitely be fun! 

Town Hall

In Amsterdam we chose to move the End User TAB Town Hall to the project pavilion and that was well received. So we’re keeping it this way and you can come and ask us questions right next to where the projects are located.

Poster sessions

Did you know Kubecon has a poster session? It’s an ideal setting to have more in-depth discussions with the authors and there are several end user focused presentations this time around.

And as always, see below for recommendations on interesting content for end users from the members of the TAB.


Joseph Sandoval

  • Surviving the Churn: Read Replicas and Controllers for Busy Kubernetes Clusters (Nov 10, 12:20 PM, Salt Palace, Grand Ballroom ACE). Your apiserver is one ordered log with everyone yelling at it, and when watchers fall behind, they get 410 Gone and relist, which makes it worse. Anthropic’s war story: one innocent LIST sent a cluster of tens of thousands of nodes into a doom spiral, twice in two weeks. Some of us have the scars.
  • N Clusters, One kubectl: Multi-Cluster That Just Works (Nov 10, 3:40 PM, Hyatt Regency, Salt Lake Ballroom C). OCM-style multi-cluster fixes the fleet problem and creates a developer problem: the hub template is the source of truth, so the kubectl scale you just ran quietly gets reverted. Salesforce and NVIDIA built a proxy that makes the fleet feel like one cluster again, kubectl edit included. Every platform fix sends a bill to somebody else, and this talk shows what it took to pay that one down.
  • Anatomy of an Outage: When Bursty ML Workloads Break the Kubernetes Scheduler (Nov 11, 11:00 AM, Salt Palace, Grand Ballroom H). Pending workloads timed out webhooks and took down a control plane, which probably looked fine in the design review. Isomorphic Labs and Google walk through how they stabilized it with decoupled queues and Kueue tuning. I’m looking forward to reviewing the receipts.
  • Hardening Kubernetes for GovCloud: A 3-Year Journey to FedRAMP Moderate Authorization (Nov 11, 11:50 AM, Salt Palace, Grand Ballroom ACE). Three years to an ATO sounds about right to anyone who has argued with an auditor over a deploy pipeline. Kudos to the Verkada team for building their own deployment system to meet the isolation rules, then taking on FedRAMP’s patching mandates. If you work in a regulated environment or are working on it, be front and center for the lessons learned.

Juliano Martinez

  • Zero Downtime CNI Migration at Scale: Canal to Cilium Across Hundreds of Production Clusters (Nov 10,  4:40 PM, Salt Palace,  Level 1, 151). Migrating a CNI plugin in production is one of the most high-risk operations in Kubernetes infra. At Walmart running hundreds of clusters across cloud and on-premises environments, the team faced route-drop failures in Flannel beyond 300 nodes, iptables rule explosion as services grew and etcd v2 incompatibility blocking upgrades. No published playbook existed for zero-downtime CNI replacement at that scale.
  • Saturated by Design – Maximizing Cluster Allocation in On-Premises Kubernetes (Nov 10, 11:30 AM). On-premises compute is inelastic, and the costs are mostly up-front. Yet workload demands and hardware health can change at any time. How do you make the most of your on-premises investments without risking capacity overruns and potential outages?
  • Running Secure Agents at Scale (Nov 11, 5:00 PM, Salt Palace, Level 1, Grand Ballroom GI). Building secure and scalable agents at scale is hard. From multi-tenancy and noisy-neighbor risk to tool access and data boundaries, teams need more than a prompt and a container image; they need a deliberate execution model.
  • From Packets to Paychecks: eBPF-Based Network Cost Attribution at Scale (Nov 12, 11:50 AM, Salt Palace, Level 1, Grand Ballroom BDF). Cloud provider bills show egress costs as a single line item-they don’t say which tenant caused them. At Adobe, we answer that across 400K pods in 31K namespaces spanning 85+ multi-tenant Kubernetes clusters using Retina eBPF agents to capture pod-level flows at the kernel. Prometheus enriches them with node topology, and a CIDR-based classifier maps each destination IP to a cost category (Local, Internet, Peering, Transit Gateway, VPC Endpoint) with cross-AZ and cross-region modifiers that align to cloud provider billing.

Kenta Tada

  • Lessons Learned Sandboxing Agents with kagent
    • AI agents may look like ordinary Kubernetes workloads, but their long-lived, stateful, and highly privileged behavior makes sandboxing a fundamentally different challenge. This session shares lessons from building agent sandboxing with kagent, covering filesystem and tool access, credentials, networking, identity, and cleanup, along with how NVIDIA’s OpenShell, Kubernetes’ agent-sandbox, and Google’s substrate support shape the design.
  • GPU Observability with eBPF: From Kernel Hooks to Kubernetes Metrics
    • GPUs are becoming a critical resource in Kubernetes, yet understanding what is happening on them remains a black box. This session shows how to build production-grade GPU observability with eBPF, from hooking into GPU interfaces and enriching telemetry with Kubernetes context to packaging programs as OCI images and integrating metrics with Prometheus and OpenTelemetry.

Chad Beaudin – Boeing

  • Birds of a Feather: Public Sector user Group
    • The Public Sector user group recently went through the new process to be recognized as an official CNCF user group.  They have been a healthy user group for a few years and I’m excited to sit in on their BoF session and hear the latest challenges (and solutions!) that leaders in that industry face.
  • Hallway Track
    • It’s cliche for a reason.  I get so much value from talking to fellow practitioners at Kubecon.  This is where I get to really find out what their pain points are, what worked for them, what their recommendations are for MY problems.
  • Project Pavillion
    • I love hitting the project pavilion to talk to the newer projects in the sandbox and incubation tiers. KubeCon is the one place I can talk directly to maintainers about where their project is headed, what adoption looks like in the wild, and where the technical gaps are.

Ricardo Rocha

  • Why We Bet the Data Platform on Kubernetes – And How AI Is Changing How We Operate It

Whether you already integrated agents in your ops stack, have them reporting and recommending actions, or are thinking about it, come and listen how others are doing it
